"Homage to the supreme God of gods! Homage indeed to Mahādeva! / Homage to the destroyer of the limbs of Kāma! Homage indeed to the blue-throated one! / Homage to the destroyer of Tuṣita, and to the subduer of the three worlds! / Homage to the foremost staff of Time, homage indeed to the terrible staff!"
To him whose hands and feet are everywhere, whose eyes and faces are everywhere, / to him who rules over all, who abides encompassing everything.
Homage to you who are gold-hued and beyond the senses; / homage to the golden liṅga, homage indeed to the universal liṅga.
Homage to him whose color is like the moon and sun, to the lord of yoga, the unconquered one, / to him whose hand holds the Pināka bow, and whose hands bear the trident and the club.
To the quiver-bearer, the sword-bearer, and the bearer of the battle-axe, / to the charioteer, the shield-bearer, and indeed homage to Maheśa.
Homage to him whose hand holds the three-pronged spear, the bearer of the fierce staff; / homage to the lord of the gaṇas, homage to the lord of the Rudras.

Homage to him with a thousand eyes, homage indeed to him with a hundred eyes; / to the lord of the Ādityas, homage to the lord of the Vasus.
Homage to the lord of the earth, homage to the lord of space;
homage to the lord of the heavenly world, homage to the husband of Umā.
Homage to him who is reachable through yoga, the granter of all yoga, / who is meditated upon by meditators and praised by meditators.
To Death, the staff of Time, to Yama, and to the Great Soul; / to the overlord of the gods, and to him of divine form.
To the sacrifice, the giver of wealth, the bestower of heaven, and to victory; / to the sun among all the gods, to Dharma of multiform shapes;
to the immortal, the choice one, praised by all deities, / who severed the head of Brahmā and the head of the great sacrifice.

To the destroyer of Tripura, the fierce one, the remover of all inauspiciousness; / to him whose half-body is the form of Umā, whose eye is on the forehead.
To the slayer of Mahiṣa and Andhaka, the seer, Parameṣṭhin; / to the holy teacher, the generator of Brahmā;
to the teacher of Kumāra, the granter of boons to Kumāra;
to the bearer of the plow, the crusher with the pestle, homage to him of great laughter.
To him in whose hands is the snare of Death, whose sacred thread is Takṣaka; / to him accompanied by lightning, clouds, and wind, who likewise rides upon a bull.
To the dweller on the Himavat and the Vindhya, the dweller on the back of Meru, / the dweller on Kailāsa, and the companion of the Lord of Wealth.
To him who yielded half his body to Viṣṇu, who gave boons to him; / to the lord of sacrifice of all beings, compassionate to all beings.

To the primeval being within all beings, the giver of life to living creatures; / homage to you who think, and indeed to consciousness itself.
To the one who is known, the object of knowledge, the seer, homage to the eye; / homage to you who cause perception by touch, and likewise to taste.
Homage to smell and the smeller, to the ear and the hearer; / to the hand-possessor and the hand, and likewise to the foot-possessor and the foot.
Homage to the maker of joy, and homage to you who are joy; / to speech and to the eloquent speaker, to the Great Soul who is the subtle elements.
Homage to the subtle and to the gross, to sattva and to rajas; / homage continually to austerity, to the knower of the field, the unconquered one.
To Viṣṇu, the creator of the world, homage to the lord of creatures; / homage to the seven sages, to the one who is tormented and to the ascetic.

To him who is gracious to brahmins and […], homage likewise to Durvāsas; / to the craftsman, the lord of crafts, the wise Viśvakarman.
Homage to you who are Atri, Bhṛgu, and Vasiṣṭha; / to the existent one, the lord of beings, homage to the lord of […]
To him who stands, who runs, who sings, and who dances; / to the unrestrainable, the invulnerable, the ageless, and the immortal.
To the imperishable, to the one into whom all dissolves, and to the unimpeded; / who cannot be possessed by anyone, whose nature is both the visible and the invisible.
To the subtlest of the subtle, the lord of all, the Great Soul; / homage to you, O Lord, who are without eyes, homage to you, O Lord Śiva!
Homage to you, O Lord of all the worlds, homage to the creator of the worlds! / I do not desire dominion over the gods, nor the status of Brahmā,
nor the status of Viṣṇu, O Lord of gods, nor the status of Indra, O protector of beings! / I desire, O Īśāna, to be your attendant eternally and imperishably.
I desire always to see you, O Lord of gods, together with your attendants, with the Mother, gracious and accompanied by your retinue; / let this boon be granted to me!

Having formerly granted me a refuge, O God, you [prevent] rebirth; / and you, O Lord, are my refuge; I see no other anywhere.
For one abandoned by you, there is swift destruction; of this there is no doubt. / I see no other refuge; I will go near you who are auspicious.
Devoted and loving, dedicated to you and taking refuge in you, / accept me always, O God; let this boon be granted to me!

And whoever hears this constantly, or causes it to be heard among the twice-born, / attains the fruit of an aśvamedha and is honored in the world of Rudra.
Having heard even once this hymn that destroys sins, / wherever he may die, O Vyāsa, he will not come to a bad state.
He who, with restrained self, continually recites this foremost hymn and worships the deity— / what need has he of various sacrifices, gifts, sacred fords, or well-performed austerities?
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the Skandapurāṇa.

Then Hara addressed that sacred, three-streamed river. / Having seen that three-streamed river, the bull was filled with supreme joy // 25 // / and roared; and from that roar, another river arose.

therefore the one whose banner bears a bull addressed her as Ḍhiṅkārikā. / The god fastened on him his own wonderful, exceedingly marvelous crown / made of gold, and two ear-rings born of nectar. / Having seen him thus honored in the sky, a sun-like cloud, // 27–28

7.3.m:
This is known as the Pañcanada ('Five Rivers'), located near Japyeśvara; / the fruit of these, beginning with Jaṭodā, has been explained by the great-souled one. // 32 // / Having gone to that divine Pañcanada and to that god Japyeśvara, / fasting for three nights, having bathed and worshipped the wielder of the trident, // 33
and having gratified the brahmins, a man dying wherever / shall become a follower of Nandīśvara and dwell in the Ocean of Milk. // 34
And he who casts away his hard-to-abandon life-breaths at Japyeśvara, / whether by vow or otherwise, shall become my Gaṇa-leader. (35)
Equal to Nandīśvara, eternal indeed, indestructible, imperishable, / and a companion by my side, beloved and truly esteemed. (36)
Whatever human being arrives at Japyeśvara and that Pañcanada and gives up his body / shall always be my foremost Gaṇa-leader, equal to Tvaṣṭṛ, and constantly having a lovely form. (37) / Thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the Skandapurāṇa.

“O goddess, I shall consecrate the god Nandīśvara as the protector of beings; / I shall summon the Gaṇas. What do you think, O imperishable one?” (2)
The goddess said:
“The sovereignty over the seven worlds, and likewise over the Gaṇa-chiefs— / he deserves all, O Lord of gods; Nandī is my eldest son.” (3)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that blessed god, the slayer of the foes of the gods, / facing the east, called upon the chiefs of the Gaṇas then. (4) / Thereupon, in thousands, the superintendents of the Gaṇas, endowed with joy, / the lords of all worlds, arrived in that very instant, O great sage. (5)
The lords of all the worlds who arrived are the Rudras dwelling in heaven; / and there were other foremost Rudras, O Vyāsa, of whom there is no counting. (6) / And those who are the coverings of the cosmic egg, Ahirbudhnya and the rest, O sage, / Kapālins, Viśokas, having a hundred eyes, having a hundred faces, (7)

Surrounded by a hundred crores, he then saw that leader of the gaṇas. / Then another, of gentle form, with limbs smeared with ash, / carrying a trident in hand, sky-clad, endowed with the power of great yoga,
assuming many guises, devoted to the yoga of meditation, / known as Somavarṇa, surrounded by a hundred crores, a lord, / the commander of such [beings], arrived when summoned by the god.
His limbs covered with ashes from a thousand flames, having large eyes and an erect phallus.

7.3.m:
Megha, garlanded with lightning, arrived surrounded by ninety; / and Prabhākara with twenty, and Viṭpati of great strength; / Girika, Meghanāda, Udara, and Maṇi;
divine-souled Kāṣṭhakarṇa, and renowned Viśvarūpa; / Śatamanyu likewise, and powerful Pañcākṣa; / Tālaketu, Shaṇḍa, Kapālī, Gajanāśana; / Saṃvartaka, Caitra, Trailokyadahana,
Lokāntaka of blazing spirit, and Hemakuṇḍala.
And Mṛtyu, and Yama, and Kāla, and Viṣahara,
Śatamāya, Mahāmāya, and Sarvatrāśaraṇa; (67)
and the renowned Ekaśṛṅga, and also Bhṛṅgiriṭi—
these and other leaders of the gaṇas, the secret ones possessing great might. (68)

Śambhu, with a deep voice, thus addressed the creator of the worlds: (83)

bestow consecration upon Nandī, who is so dear to me.” (84)

Śakra, mounted on Airāvata, arrived near him, (86)
along with the Vasus, the Mothers, Yama, Varuṇa, and the lord of riches [Kubera], (87a)
and covering the sky, stationed in individual aerial chariots. (87b)
At the end of the dissolution and in creation, under the name […],
these who had reached the form of Brahmā and the rest arrived in the form of gaṇas. (88)
They, radiant as a thousand suns, bowed to Viśvakarman, the laugher at enemies, the lord of the universe, the imperishable single syllable, and cried out aloud. (89)
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, entitled “The Summoning of the Leaders of the Gaṇas,” in the Skandapurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Those lords of the gaṇas, beings of great strength, having bowed to the lord of the gods of all the gods,
and to the god of gods, spoke these words: (1)
“O Blessed One, destroyer of the enemies of the gods, god of gods, husband of Ambikā,
for what purpose have we been summoned? Command us, for it is as good as done! (2)

Shall we dry up the oceans, or Yama together with Rāhu's attendants?
Shall we slay Mṛtyu and Kāla? None of them is unborn compared to him! (3)
Having bound Indra together with the gods, and Viṣṇu along with Vāyu,
shall we bring them, or, intensely enraged, the Daityas together with the Dānavas? (4)
Whose terrible ruin shall we bring about today by your command?
Or for whom, O God, shall we make a festival today that abounds in the fulfillment of all desires?” (5)
To all of them speaking thus and bowing, the lover of devotees,
the god Bhava, lord of the gaṇas, having honored the gaṇas, spoke: (6)
The god of gods said:
“Hear, you who bring welfare to the universe, that for the sake of which you have been summoned here,
and having heard, with restrained minds, carry it out without hesitation. (7)
This Nandīśvara is our son, O lords of lords over all;
he is dear to you, a foremost leader, and your steadfast general. (8)

7.3.m:
And to the son of Śilāda, devoted to Rudra's mantra, / to the god devoted to Rudra, praise to him who rests within the water!
Praise to the lord of gaṇas, and to the lord of beings, / to the god who is the son of Umā, who has obtained boons from Śiva!
To the beloved son of Rudra, who bears the paṭṭiśa weapon, / praise to him who has terrifying fangs, and who has an eye on his forehead!
To the foremost attendant, the excellent one, offered to Īśāna, / to the guardian of the doorway, the heroic one, to Rudra who grants boons!
Praise to him by whom all aims are accomplished, praise to the lord of Suyaśā! / Praise to him who has an excellent garland, who dwells in the ocean of milk!
To the supreme lord of gaṇas, and to the supreme lord of yoga, / whose head resounds with the diṇḍima drum, the fierce one, devoted to the single syllable [Oṃ]!
To the imperishable, to the unchangeable, to the unaging, to the immortal, / and to the lord of creatures, and likewise the conqueror of death!

Having thus praised him, O Vyāsa, the god, with cupped hands and composed mind, / uttered the cry of victory to that great-souled one.
Then the gaṇas said, “Victory!”, then the gods, then the suras, / then all living beings, and likewise Brahmā and Śakra.
Then conches, kettledrums, paṭaha and āḍambara drums, / flutes, paṇava drums, kṛkavā-horns, and cow horns,
diṇḍima drums, reeds, and mardala drums on all sides, / the leaders of gaṇas played, causing joy, filled with gladness.
Sanatkumāra said:
A mortal who would constantly recite this hymn to Nandīśvara, / composed by the gods, would go to his realm.
He who goes to sleep having uttered, “Praise to Nandīśvara!”,

Sanatkumāra said:
Then the god Bhava, the lord of deities, the righteous protector, / having honored the Maruts who had arrived there, spoke always for the sake of a maiden:
Addressing by name the Maruts who possess great speed, great strength, and great power, / the Lord [Śiva], accompanied by Śakra and the Grandsire [Brahmā], [said]:
“You ought to give, with honor, your maiden Suyaśā, Sanasā, of divine form; / she shall be the daughter-in-law of us two.”
The Maruts said:
“You are the ruler of us, of her, / and of the entire world, O Lord of the three worlds; you ought not to ask of us.
She is yours to give and yours to take; you are our unsurpassed resort.

7.3.m:
Do not treat us as strangers, O Īśāna, by begging from us!
Our father is the glorious Kaśyapa, and Marīci is our grandfather; / the father of our grandfather is Brahmā, and you are even his great father.
That you are our great-grandfather; you ought not to make us out to be strangers.”
Īśvara said:
“You are not strangers to us; the truth has been spoken by you. / Yet it has been declared by sages and gods for the welfare of the world:
A maiden should not be taken unbestowed; this is eternal dharma.”

7.3.m:
Thus praised by all the lords of the gaṇas, the lord Nandīśvara, / bowing down, said to them all: “Speak! What may I do for you?” / Having been addressed thus, all those exceedingly mighty lords of the gaṇas, / knowing divine matters, spoke to him in the presence of the God of gods:
“You have been made our gaṇa-commander by Lord Śambhu, / and consecrated by us as leader, the giver of dharma. / As such, be auspicious, gentle, and endowed with virtues even among those devoid of virtue; / endowed with forbearance, purity, and self-restraint, always do what is pleasing to us!”
Sanatkumāra said:

Homage, homage to the supreme yogins and to the matted-haired! / Homage to you of visible forms, and likewise to the deformed! / Homage to those clothed in bark garments, and to those clothed in animal hides!
Homage to those with white robes and garlands, homage, homage to those with variegated garlands! / Homage, homage to those running, those rushing, and those standing firm! / Homage to the sages, to those singing, and homage, homage to those chanting!
Homage to those in the form of a śarabha, and to those of a hundred forms! / Homage to those in the form of mountains, and to those in the form of tigers! / Homage to those in the form of cats, and to crows and owls! / Homage to those in the form of deities, and likewise to the winds! / Homage to the fires, and likewise to the waters and to the Varuṇas!
Homage to those in the form of Dhaneśa, and to those of all forms! / Homage to those whose mouths are on their bellies, and to those with all mouths! / Homage to those of dwarfish form, and to those who take any form at will!

Then what did Mahādeva, the lord who grants desires, do, / seated there with the goddess? This I desire to know. (2)
Sanatkumāra said:
On the peak of the Himālaya, the Lord Śarva, wishing to please the goddess, / repeatedly provoking laughter with the gaṇa-lords of diverse forms, / he who bears the crescent moon as his crest delighted the goddess and took delight / with his glorious, omniscient, auspicious [attendants] who assume shapes at will. (3–4)
Then the supreme goddess went alone to her mother, / who was seated on a bright golden, well-prepared seat of high honor. (5) / Seeing Satī, the goddess of auspicious form, who had arrived, / she honored that blameless one with a costly seat. (6)
And to her seated there Menā, the beloved of the Himālaya, said: / 'After a long time indeed is your coming today, O daughter with auspicious eyes! (7) / For your husband plays in companionship with games of beggars; / those who are poor and likewise destitute,
O Umā, play in such a manner as your husband does, O auspicious one.' (8)

Nikumbha too, having achieved his purpose, the lord standing in the sky, / spoke to that Divodāsa, as if burning him with his splendour: / 'The gods grant the desired boon according to one's wish. / If it was not given, what anger was that on your part?'
'Since my temple has been broken by you when I had done no wrong, / therefore your city shall be desolate for a thousand years.'

incurred supreme shame, and then went to his palace.
Then, through that curse, the city of Vārāṇasī at once / became empty, cleared, haunted only by wild beasts.

In that vimāna endowed with every prosperity and inaccessible to speech, / the daughter of the king of mountains, whose blossoming eyes resembled fresh blue lotuses, took her pleasure, / and the goddess did not remember the words of her own mother. / Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, named 'The Desolation of Vārāṇasī', in the Skandapurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, as the two of them, the daughter of the mountain and the bull-bannered [god], were seated happily / on that divine golden throne adorned with various jewels, / then the goddess, the daughter of the mountain, sitting at ease, radiant, / the daughter of the king of mountains, said to her husband, the lord of all worlds:
'O Blessed One, destroyer of the enemies of the gods, adorned with the crescent moon! / Tell me this, O all-pervading lord, what I ask of you, O bestower of honor!
What fruit do your devotees obtain, O lord of gods, O compassionate to devotees, / when they do nothing aiming at a reward?'
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus addressed by Umā, the trident-handed, bull-bannered / god of gods, unagitated, spoke of all that is auspicious and inauspicious. / Vyāsa said:

What was that which the blessed god, pleased, of great austerity, / the imperishable one, thus questioned with love by the goddess, recounted?

7.3.m:
'Let it be heard; I will declare what you ask me, O faithful lady. / Questioned for the benefit of devotees, O goddess, I shall explain it to you. / Whoever, O unblemished goddess, builds a white temple for me, / I prepare for him a bright, imperishable house in the city of Śiva.
And whoever establishes a liṅga of mine according to the prescribed rule / roams constantly with me, endowed with the eight supernatural powers. / Whoever offers me gold, even merely a particle or in great quantity, / I give him an excellent home on the Himalayan peak.
Whoever, with a cheerful heart, offers me a cow or gold, O beloved, / to him I give worlds endowed with all desires. / Whoever offers me a bull, either white or dark blue, / he redeems twenty-one generations of both families.
And whoever gives me a plot of land of the measure of two gocarmas, / he, having reached my city, rejoices with the lords of the gaṇas.

Whatever fruit is traditionally stated for giving a thousand bilva leaves to me, / he obtains that fruit when a single baka flower is offered to me.
Whatever fruit is gained when a thousand baka flowers are offered to me, / he obtains that when a single dhattūra flower is offered.
The man who constantly places my nirmālya upon his head, / if impure, transgressing propriety, endowed with sin, / self-willed, unrestrained, and excluded from vows, / falls into a dreadful hell and is reborn in an animal womb.
But he who, having become a celibate student and pure, wears the nirmālya, / his sin I quickly destroy, O lady of great vows!
Whoever arranges a row of lamps for me in the month of Kārttika, / and at the conclusion of the lamps, being pure, satisfies brahmins,
He obtains the status of Gaṇapati and shines like the sun. / He should also offer black sesame seeds and white mustard seeds.

7.3.m:
I am not pleased when worshipped in an image, O goddess, daughter of the mountain, / to the extent that I am exceedingly delighted when worshipped in the liṅga, O Pārvatī. / Whether attached to all the senses or bound by all sins, / he goes to heaven, O goddess, who worships my liṅga here.
Abandoning all sins, free from dualities, his transgressions burned away, / resting in my blessings, saluting me, he attains Me alone.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then the goddess asked her husband again, the Lord of all the world: / ‘[…] By what are you pleased, O Lord?’ / Thereupon, his face smiling, the Lord of all lords of the world, / the Blessed Lord, spoke these words wishing the welfare of the worlds.
The God of Gods said:
Listen in truth, O goddess, [to that] by which all living beings / in the three worlds who are devoted to me attain an auspicious state, O fair-faced one.
Whatever supreme secret there is, all that abides in me. / He who knows that in truth is freed from saṃsāra.

7.3.m:
The devoted person should never cause this to be heard by an inauspicious one, nor by a sinner,
nor by an untruthful one, nor by one without vows, nor by one devoid of merit.
It bestows fortune, fame, longevity; it increases peace; it is auspicious,
purified, supreme purifier, and the most auspicious of auspicious things.
It must not be heard by everyone, nor should it be given to just anyone.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, named 'The Worship of Īśvara', in the Skandapurāṇa.
Vyāsa said:
"Having thus in time attained an abode in Vārāṇasī,
what did the two gods, the parents of the universe, do after this?"
Sanatkumāra said:
"Then that blessed god said to the goddess,
the daughter of the Himālaya: 'O goddess, let us see the pleasure garden, if it pleases you.'"
The goddess said:
"So be it, O Lord of gods, as you have spoken, O Bull-bannered One.
Indeed, I have nowhere else to go beyond the garden, O Hara."

filled with campaka, aśoka, punnāga, priyaṅgu, and mango trees,
and with bilva, arjuna, kadamba, nyagrodha, and udumbara trees.

a perfected mortal grieves no more over death and birth. / All around, liṅgas have indeed been established by all the deities. . . 39 ..

and worships Saṃgameśāna, whence has he any fear of rebirth? / This other great sacred field is the supreme dwelling of yogins,
wherein I, having manifested myself, abide in the center of the sacred field; / it is renowned among all gods and demons as Madhyameśvara.

7.3.m:
This sacred field is proclaimed to extend one krośa in the four directions. / […] O lovely-limbed one, it grants immortality at the time of death.
[…] situated in the abode of Kedāra; / having seen it, the state of a Gaṇa is attained, and in this sacred field liberation is gained.
From that rank of a Gaṇa, supreme liberation arises; / beyond Mahālaya, beyond Kedāra, and even beyond Madhyama,
this Avimukta is remembered as the most sacred field, O auspicious one. / Kedāra and Madhyama are places, and so too is Mahālaya,
sacred places of mine on earth, yet this is the most supreme of them. / When the worlds were destroyed, then this auspicious sacred field
was never abandoned by me; therefore it became Avimukta. / A person who beholds my liṅga Avimukteśvara here,
is immediately freed from sin and released from the bonds of individual souls. / Śaileśa, Saṃgameśa, Svalīna, and Madhyameśvara,

filled on all sides with splendors like those of fire and the sun. / Then the perfected Pāśupatas, radiant white with the smearing of ashes,
great-souled masters of yoga, observers of the Vedic ritual vows, / wearing unmanifest marks, radiant with the splendor of Śiva's yoga, / many approaching at once, bowed down to Maheśvara.
Gazing again upon the Lord of Gods and fully upon yoga of meditation, / they stood, having steadied their selves, as if dissolving into Īśvara. / As they stood thus, the God of Gods, the lord of Umā,
contemplating the supreme form, the sovereign Lord became the Puruṣa, / the twenty-sixth principle, the unmanifest Īśvara, equal in splendor to tens of thousands of suns.
He stood, as if intent on bringing the whole universe together into one.
As the Lord of the Universe assumed that supreme form,
the daughter of the king of mountains, her body bristling with hair standing on end, was unable to look upon his body.

Then those yogins, effecting their dissolution into Puruṣa,
entered his heart, all the seeds of worldly existence burned away.
Then, having bestowed grace upon all those perfected beings, foremost among ascetics,
he made his auspicious body dwell once more in the form of Nīlalohita.

Having seen that, the daughter of the mountain, every hair on her body bristling with joy,
went [forward] praising his two feet, and said, “Who are these, O Blessed One?”
Then the best among gods spoke to the goddess, the daughter of the king of mountains:
“By the foremost twice-born devoted [to me], having undertaken my vow,
by whichever [of them] yoga was practiced here, to them, in a single lifetime,
through the power of this sacred field and through devotion arising from contemplation on me,
grace is indeed thus bestowed by me, ever granting liberation.
Therefore this great sacred field of mine is resorted to by Brahmā and the others,
and by the foremost brahmins learned in the Vedas, and by perfected ascetics,
every month on the eighth, and every month on the fourteenth,
in both fortnights, O goddess, in Vārāṇasī, my abode,
and at eclipses of the moon and sun, especially on the full-moon day of Kārttika,
on all auspicious festive days, and at the equinoxes and solstices.
All the sacred fords on earth [resort] to the Jāhnavī in Vārāṇasī,

This secret, ever most holy sacred field of mine, O daughter of the Snowy Mountain,
which grants the fruit of griefless perfection, ascetics who have awakened to truth worship.
Those virtuous devotees, men who dwell always in this sacred field [devoted] to me—
beholding [me] daily with respect, pure, having bathed, ever intent on me, / those mortals, freed from fear, sin, and sorrow, with their actions purified, / breaking through the impenetrable thicket of the snare of worldly existence, attain supreme liberation.
Thus this sacred field of mine, filled with gods, crowded with various trees and creepers, / adorned by the Jāhnavī, is most secret. / Reaching the Bhāgīrathī here, in Vārāṇasī, my abode, / obtaining [the fruit of] a hundred horse-sacrifices, one goes to the world of Brahmā.

There is nothing more sacred than this, O goddess, nowhere anything more secret than this; / there is nothing more auspicious than this, nothing dearer to me than this. / Having reached this sacred field of mine frequented by gods and siddhas, a mortal, through the power of good deeds, / becomes celebrated among all gods and asuras, and upon dying goes to that supreme abode.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter in the Skandapurāṇa.

He then saw a brahmin performing supreme austerity, / the son of Śataśalāka, Jaigīṣavya, rich in tapas. / Having consecrated a liṅga of the God of gods and worshipping it constantly, / lying on ashes, smeared with ashes, he pleased [him] with dances and songs.
Purified through recitation [of mantras], roarings of a bull, and austerity, he was pure. / As he was acting thus, endowed with supreme devotion,
the Lord approached swiftly and spoke this word: / 'O Jaigīṣavya of great intellect, behold me with divine sight!
I am pleased and I grant boons; speak what is in your mind.' / Thus addressed by the God, having seen Soma with three eyes, / bowing his head at his feet, he spoke with supreme joy:
Jaigīṣavya said:
Obeisance to the one who has attained all ends, obeisance indeed to the one accomplished in yoga! / Obeisance to the one holding the Pināka bow, and dwelling on the Himavat mountain!
Obeisance to the one swift as the wind, always to be meditated upon by meditators! / Obeisance to Soma, to the gold-like one, and to the wearer of a golden garland!

For one night, [he attains] a pure state; for two, he delivers his ancestors; / through three nights he delivers those who have passed away and seven subsequent [generations]. / What more than this today, O Jaigīṣavya, shall I give you?'
Jaigīṣavya said:
"O Lord, ruler of the gods of gods, may the desire that is in my mind be granted. / I wish for nothing other than that supreme, imperishable Yoga. / May there be constant devotion in You, together with Umā and Gaṇeśa, the Lord of Gaṇas, / and also freedom from pride, patience, tranquil restraint of mind, and control of the senses.
And may I never suffer humiliation, nor face contempt of my radiant power. / These are the boons, O God of great splendor, that I always desire."
The God of gods said:
"These shall be yours, as well as being unconquerable by yogins; / and whenever you desire it, you shall also have a vision of Me."
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that blessed Lord, O son of Parāśara, along with Umā, / with Nandin and with the Gaṇas, desiring to bestow grace upon His devotee,
holding the Yakṣa king in His heart while he was performing austerities, / went before him at that time to grant boons.

Then, beholding the Lord of gods accompanied by the Mother and preceded by Nandin, / he bowed, but being utterly emaciated, he was unable to stand up. / Observing him weak and incapable of rising, the Lord / said: "Arise, may all be well with you! Let your former strength return to you!"
Then, rising onto his knees, Kubera indeed stood up, / and he remained looking at the Goddess standing by His side with his eye:
"This is that daughter of the mountain, bowed to by all the worlds, / mother of these three worlds, endowed with the power of great yoga! / Ah, the power of Her austerity! Ah, Her radiance! Ah, Her strength! / She who indeed became the wife of the Lord of all the worlds!"
Sanatkumāra said:
The Goddess perceived him with such a mind gazing upon Pārvatī, / and having perceived it, the Supreme Goddess became enraged.
Growing angry, She burned Kubera's brightly radiant left eye, / just as a blazing flame of fire consumes dry brushwood.
Moreover, that fair-faced lady, the source of austerities, resolved in mind to destroy Kubera; / thereupon Hara spoke to Her:

"O Goddess, do not be angry with this Yakṣa, who is Your devoted ascetic. / He is renowned, righteous, and especially devoted to You.
Indeed, it was out of curiosity that he looked at You, O auspicious one! / Grant favor to the child, the giver of wealth, O Great Goddess!"
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of gods, this one repeatedly looks upon Me out of insolence, O master! / He does not diminish My virtues, O God, yet why does he stand before Me?
He who out of delusion oversteps those of immeasurable splendor, / being of little power, shall perish, like a moth entering fire."
Sanatkumāra said:
Seeing Śaṃkara's consort angry in this way, her eyes red with wrath, / He spoke sweet and gentle words to the daughter of the king of mountains: / "I tell You, O highly blessed one, do not be angry, O battle-ground of the world! / All the universe was created by You; You are Prakṛti, O ruler of the gods!

Homage to the Earth, the Auspicious, to Śrī, to Lakṣmī, homage, homage! / Homage to the Nectar, to Svāhā, to Svadhā, to Diti, homage!
Homage be to the Lightning and to the Flash of Lightning, homage, homage! / And then to Savitṛ, to Gāyatrī, to the Mother of the Vedas, homage, homage!
Homage to the Daughter of the Mountain, to Intellect, to Memory, homage! / Homage to the Mountain-Dweller, and to Rudrāṇī homage, homage!
Homage to Nature, and to Moonlight, to Prosperity, homage! / To Splendor, to Radiance, and to the Ray of the Sun-Planet!

To Motion, to the Goal, and to Indrāṇī, to Liberation, homage! / To Destiny, to the River, and to Gaṅgā, to the Origin, homage!
To the Cause, and to Delight, homage to the functioning of the sense organs! / Homage to Continuity, and to the Earth, to Livelihood, homage!
To Vāruṇī, and to the Refuge, to Peace, to Beauty, homage, homage! / And homage be to Kauśikī, to Kātyāyanī homage, homage!
Homage to Humility, and to Greatness homage, homage! / Homage be to Minuteness, to Lightness homage, homage!
And homage to you as Worship, and to the White-Armed One, and to Creeping Motion, / and homage be to Consciousness, to Speech, and then to Memory, homage!
Homage be to Sarasvatī, to the Tongue, to Sight, homage!
Homage to the Slayer of Mahiṣa, and likewise of Śumbha and Niśumbha!
Homage to her who rides a lion, and to the Spear-Bearer homage, homage! / Homage to the Mace-Bearer, to the Armored One homage, homage!
Homage to the Earring-Wearer, to the Upholder of the universe, homage!

Homage to the Auspicious One, and to the Maker, to Power homage, homage! / To Mṛkaṇḍu, and to the Soft-Armed One, and likewise to Surabhi, homage!
To Vinatā, and likewise to Lakṣmī, to Surasā homage, homage! / Homage to you with a dark throat, homage to you everywhere, always!
Being well-disposed, grant us all whatever is in our heart!
Sanatkumāra said:
The man or woman who recites this daily with concentrated mind / will completely cast off all sin committed in the nights.
And he who, lying down, regularly recites it with restraint, O Vyāsa, / will shed [sin] committed by day, and when dead, will go to a good destination.

7.3.m:
And he who listens to this daily, or always makes brahmins hear it, / reaching the destruction of the body, will become beloved of the apsarases.
And if a mortal reciting this repeatedly casts off his life, so hard to abandon,
in an aerial chariot resembling the sun, served by groups of apsarases, / freed from all sins, he will rejoice for a million years.
And a person observing vows who, with supreme devotion, on the lunar day,
having worshipped the Goddess, recites [it], is liberated from all sins.
Through recitation alone, by austerity, when the body has dissolved, that devoted one, / having become an attendant of the Goddess, is glorified in the holy realm.
Sanatkumāra said:
Praised by them, the Goddess, standing in the presence of the God, / rejoiced, her face radiant, and spoke these words to the Pañcacūḍā [apsarases]: / 'Listen, all you apsarases, to the great fruit of this austerity, / and because you, auspicious ones, have taken refuge in me with supreme devotion. // 124–125

Ageless, free from sorrow, ever joyful in mind, / and dear to the whole world shall you be by my command. / Tell me without hesitation whatever lies in your hearts; / I shall grant it all to you—do not delay, free from distress.' // 126–127
The Pañcacūḍās said:
'O Goddess, you know that all women exist for the sake of men's needs. / They desire us only as long as their purpose is served; / and once their purpose is fulfilled, they treat us as strangers. // 128
Therefore, O Goddess, if you are pleased and if a boon is to be granted to us, / O Great Goddess, let men become subject to the control of all women.' / The Goddess said: // 129
'From this day forward in the worlds, let men always / be subject to all women everywhere, performing all their bidding. // 130

How did he become the guardian of the field (kṣetrapāla), and how did he become beloved? / O son of Brahmā, I wish to hear this narrated by you.' / Sanatkumāra said: // 2
'Listen, O Vyāsa, to how that Piṅgala obtained the leadership of the gaṇas, / the role of giver of food to the worlds, and the abode of Vārāṇasī. // 3
The glorious son of Pūrṇabhadra was a powerful yakṣa / renowned as Harikeśa, devoted to brahmins and righteous. // 4
From his very birth, he had unsurpassed devotion to Bhava (Śiva); / his blessings were for Him, his salutations to Him, steadfast in Him, devoted to Him. // 5
Sitting, lying down, walking, standing, following behind, / eating or drinking, he contemplated Rudra alone. / Seeing him thus single-minded, his father Pūrṇabhadra said: / 'I do not consider you my son, base-born one who are so contrary.' // 6–7

Sanatkumāra said:
Addressed in this way by his son, the mighty Pūrṇabhadra / said: "Get out quickly! Go wherever it pleases you!" . . 13 . . / Then, departing, he abandoned home, kin, and relatives; / having reached Vārāṇasī, he performed austere tapas difficult to perform. . . 14 . .
Motionless like a pillar, unblinking, resembling a dry log or a stone, / restraining the multitude of senses, he stood firm without moving. . . 15 . .
Then, as he remained continually devoted to that, having that as his sole blessing, / a single thousand divine years passed by. . . 16 . .

Then the Lord of the world, the maintainer of all the worlds,
together with the daughter of the snowy mountain and his beloved troop-leaders, / showed the goddess the exceedingly lovely park, / filled with diverse and broad trees and drunk, joyful cuckoos.
The goddess said:
The garden, endowed with supreme splendor, has been shown by you, O God. / But you ought to speak once more of all the virtues of the sacred field here.
Having heard repeatedly the majesty of this sacred field of Avimukta, / truly there is no satiety for me; therefore speak to me further.
The God of gods said:
This Vārāṇasī is my most secret sacred field always, / at all times the cause of liberation for all living beings whatsoever.

In this place, O goddess, perfected beings, ever dedicated to my observance, / wearing various liṅgas, desiring my world,
practice supreme yoga, focused in self and with senses conquered, / in [a place] filled with various trees and creepers, frequented by various birds,
adorned with lakes abounding in lotuses and water-lilies, / ever served by hosts of apsarases and gandharvas, auspicious.
Listen to the purpose for which dwelling here is pleasing to me: / One whose mind is fixed on me, who is devoted to me, whose all actions are offered to me,
as he attains liberation here, so [he can] nowhere else. / For those intent on recitation and meditation, and those whose minds are attached to knowledges,

7.3.m:
Because it has not been forsaken by me, nor will it ever be forsaken, / therefore this sacred field of mine is remembered as 'Avimukta'.
Since at Naimiṣa, Kurukṣetra, Gaṅgādvāra, or Puṣkara, / liberation is not attained by ritual ablution or service,
whereas it is obtained here, for this reason this [place] is superior. / Either at Prayāga liberation may occur, or here through my acceptance.
Even compared to Prayāga, the foremost of sacred fords, this very place is remembered as superior; / Jaigīṣavya, who attained the supreme perfection, was one of great austerity.
By the māhātmya of this sacred field and through devotion to me with pure intention, / the most beloved cave of Jaigīṣavya is considered the abode of yogins.
For one who meditates on me there constantly, the fire of yoga blazes brightly; / he attains the supreme kaivalya, which is difficult even for the gods to attain.

and union with myself, as well as the desired abode. / Kuvera of great being, having thus dedicated all actions [to me],

Worshipping me right here, O goddess, he will attain unsurpassed perfection: / Parāśara's son, the yogin, the seer Vyāsa of great austerity,
who will become my devotee and the establisher of the Vedic order; / he too, O lotus-eyed one, the best among sages, delights in this sacred field.
Even Brahmā along with the seers, Viṣṇu, Vāyu, the Sun, / the king of gods, Śakra, and other celestial beings,
these great souls worship the Lord of all here, O lady of good vows; / becoming single-minded, they ever worship me alone.
And Alarka, by my grace, will obtain this city; / and having restored it as before, filled with the four castes, // 8.30(2).70
prosperous / and teeming with people, and having enjoyed it for a long time, / with all his life-breaths surrendered to me, he will attain me alone.

This is remembered as my most beloved [...], O goddess, [...]
a sacred field of diverse trees and shrubs, abundant with flowers; / embodied beings who die in this [place] attain the state
known as liberation, and even Śivahood; there is no doubt in this. // 84
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, named Vārāṇasīmāhātmya, in the Skandapurāṇa.
